pattern.notes: Strict sectional timing: 40 minutes per section, fixed order VARC → DILR → QA, no switching. Mix of MCQs (+3/−1) and TITA (type-in-the-answer, +3/0, no negative marking); in this mock TITA items — para-jumble orders, odd-sentence numbers and numeric answers — are typed in (numerical type) and carry no penalty when wrong. RC passages (4 per paper, roughly 450–600 words, 4 questions each) and DILR sets (4–5 questions on one caselet) are served as complete sets. Scores are normalised across the three slots. Question count per section has varied slightly (66–68 total) between years.

trendAnalysis.summary: Since 2023 CAT has kept the 120-minute, 3×40-minute format with 66–68 questions (68 in 2024 and 2025: VARC 24, DILR 22, QA 22). VARC is dominated by four RC passages (16 questions); verbal ability is para-jumbles, odd-sentence-out and para-summary, mostly TITA. DILR has been the toughest section in 2024–2025 with four or five lengthy sets — scheduling/arrangement, tables with missing data, tournaments and set/Venn-based puzzles. QA is arithmetic- and algebra-heavy (together ≈60%), with geometry the next most important; 2025 Slot 3 QA was reported as particularly hard. Overall difficulty: moderate to difficult; selection of sets/questions matters more than speed.

pyqBlueprint.method: Compiled from slot-wise memory-based analyses and solved-paper reviews of CAT 2023, 2024 and 2025 (IMS, TIME, Career Launcher, Cracku, Hitbullseye, iQuanta and InsideIIM write-ups found via web search); IIM Lucknow/IIM Kolkata/IIM Calcutta do not publish official papers, and the full analysis pages could not be fetched, so question types were consolidated from search snippets plus the writer's own knowledge of the three papers. Every pattern is described in our own words; no actual question is reproduced.

archetypes.pattern: 450–600-word humanities/social-science/science passage with 4 questions; 'central idea / primary concern' question whose distractors seize a peripheral detail, over-generalise, or state the view the author argues against
Inference / 'the author would most likely agree' question on an argumentative passage; wrong options are extreme versions of the author's claim or statements the passage leaves untested
Function question: why the author cites a particular example, analogy or closing sentence; traps describe the example's content instead of its role in the argument
Strengthen/weaken a claim or explanation reported in the passage; the key option attacks the causal link (confounder, missing comparison), distractors support it or are irrelevant
Author's tone or attitude toward a trend or idea; options pair close adjectives (qualified scepticism vs outright hostility) so only a balanced reading fits
Detail / 'all of the following EXCEPT' question checking which listed statement the passage does not support
Meaning of a figurative phrase or key claim in context; distractors take the phrase literally or exaggerate it
4/5-sentence TITA para jumble (answer keyed in as the order of sentence numbers) built on chronology or contrast, with an opening general statement and a 'Yet/However' turn
4/5-sentence TITA para jumble locked by demonstratives ('such delays', 'those marks', 'the two groups') that cannot precede their referent; tempting orders break that chain
TITA odd sentence out: five jumbled sentences, four form a paragraph; key in the number of the sentence that shifts to a related but different subject
TITA odd sentence out where the odd sentence stays in the same broad area (same field, same era) but leaves the paragraph's specific thread
Para summary: choose the option that best captures the paragraph; distractors are too narrow, too extreme, or add a claim not in the text
Linear row seating with distance clues ('exactly two between'), adjacency, end-seat and left/right order; ask who occupies a seat
Circular seating with clockwise/anticlockwise and opposite-seat clues, single configuration to be deduced
archetypes.frequency: 1 set in two of three slots

archetypes.pattern: DILR set (4–5 questions): scheduling people/items into days or slots with counting constraints (days per person, no three consecutive, pairs together on k days); some questions add an 'if …' condition
Floors / ranking order with parity and gap clues; question asks what must be true when two arrangements survive
Multi-year table of values for several entities; compare percentage growth where the largest absolute or one-year change is the trap
Table needing a derived quantity (units × price, weighted share) before comparing; the raw-count leader is the trap
DILR set: partially specified table (scores/ratings/sales grid with row and column totals, distinct-value or range rules); reconstruct entries, some questions TITA
Round-robin league with win/draw/loss points; deduce results, minimum draws or what must be true from final points
Seeded knockout bracket with 'upset' definition; reconstruct results from counts of upsets and known finalists
Rule-based game played over rounds (players choose numbers/moves, scoring rule per round, restriction on repeating moves); reconstruct moves from final scores — 4–5 questions, some TITA
Three-set survey data (pairwise and triple overlaps or 'exactly two' counts); find exactly-one / exactly-two regions
Maximum/minimum overlap of three sets under totals; requires the exactly-one/two/three counting identity
Weighted road network (one- or two-way); shortest route, often after a road is closed
Count distinct routes in a grid or directed network, with blocked points or one-way links
Choose a team/committee under if-then and cannot-both rules; count valid selections
Approve/choose a fixed number of items under conditional rules; identify the item that must be chosen
Selection under numeric thresholds (budget, credits, score cut-offs); find valid combinations or an item common to all
Mark-up, successive discounts and profit (sometimes with false weights); solve for discount or profit %
Successive percentage changes or expenditure-consumption balance; reverse-calculate the base value
Mixture replacement (remove-and-replace, repeated) and resulting ratio/quantity
Ratio word problems: ages, partnership with changing capital × time
Relative speed: trains crossing, races with lead by distance/time
Work and efficiency: pairwise rates, efficiency multiples, alternate days, pipes
Boats and streams / two-journey simultaneous equations
SI/CI relations: CI–SI difference, amounts in consecutive years
Averages with replacement, inclusion or correction of entries
Quadratic root relations (ratio of roots, symmetric functions α/β + β/α)
Integer/natural-number solutions of linear Diophantine equations or discriminant conditions
Modulus equations/inequalities: count integer solutions, with the 'whole interval' trap
Functions: composition, functional equations, max of min(f, g) type
AP/GP: find terms or sums from two given sums/terms
Logarithmic equations with domain check (extraneous root as trap)
Surds and indices simplification / comparison
Triangle centres and radii: inradius, circumradius, incentre distances
Circle chords, tangent-secant power of a point, distance between chords
Mensuration: solids melted/recast, surface area and volume
Coordinate geometry: area of triangle/polygon from vertices, lines and intercepts
Remainders using cyclicity, Fermat/Euler or aⁿ + bⁿ divisibility by a + b
Factors: number/sum of divisors, odd/even/perfect-square divisors
Permutations/arrangements with restrictions (digits, vowels together, repeated letters)
Probability of sums/parity when drawing numbers or cards

passages.title: Passage: Knowledge from testimony
passages.text:
Most of what any of us believes about the world we have not checked. I have never measured the distance to the sun, examined the archival evidence for the date of a famous battle, or confirmed by experiment that the blood circulates. I believe these things because I was told them, by teachers, books and institutions whose reliability I am in no position to audit. Philosophers have long been uneasy about this dependence, and their unease has taken two broad forms.

The first, usually traced to Hume, holds that testimony can be a source of knowledge only derivatively. We are entitled to believe what others tell us, on this view, only to the extent that we have independent grounds — gathered through our own perception, memory and inference — for thinking that testimony of that kind tends to be true. Testimony is a conduit, not a spring; whatever warrant it carries must be paid for, eventually, in the coin of first-hand observation. The appeal of this 'reductionist' picture is that it honours an ideal of intellectual autonomy: the knower who accepts nothing she cannot, in principle, underwrite herself.

The difficulty is that the ledger never balances. A child learns the meanings of words — and so the very concepts with which she might later check a claim — by trusting the adults around her. Even an adult who sets out to verify the general reliability of, say, encyclopaedias would have to rely on testimony to learn which encyclopaedias exist, what their track record has been and how their errors were detected. The inductive base available to any single person is far too narrow to support the vast edifice of what she reasonably believes. If reductionism were true, almost all of us would know almost nothing.

The rival tradition, associated with Thomas Reid, treats our disposition to believe what we are told as a basic faculty, on a par with perception. Just as I am entitled to trust my eyes unless I have some reason to suspect them, I am entitled to accept testimony unless defeaters — signs of insincerity, incompetence or implausibility — are present. This 'anti-reductionist' view removes the impossible bookkeeping, but it purchases that relief at a price. It seems to license a kind of gullibility, sanctioning belief in whatever is asserted confidently enough until someone happens to object.

It may be that both camps have misdescribed the phenomenon by locating it in the individual. What makes it reasonable for me to believe a textbook claim about the circulation of the blood is not mainly anything I have done, nor merely an innate permission to trust, but the existence of a social structure — peer review, replication, professional sanction, the public correction of error — which filters claims before they reach me. My trust is reasonable because it is directed at a system that has been built to deserve it. This shift has an uncomfortable corollary. If the warrant for my beliefs resides largely outside my head, then the erosion of those institutions does not simply make certain sources less reliable; it quietly drains the justification from beliefs I continue to hold, without my noticing that anything has changed. Epistemic autonomy, on this account, is less a possession of the individual than an achievement of the communities that make individual trust safe.

passages.title: Passage: Reputation, courts and medieval trade
passages.text:
For a long time economic historians told a tidy story about how long-distance trade became possible before the rise of the modern state. A merchant in eleventh-century Fustat who shipped goods to an agent in Palermo faced an obvious hazard: once the cargo was out of his sight, the agent could misreport prices, skim the proceeds or simply disappear. No court in Palermo, the story went, would reliably enforce a contract on behalf of a distant foreigner. What restrained the agent was instead a private coalition. Merchants who belonged to a close-knit network shared information about one another's conduct, and an agent caught cheating any member would be shunned by all. Because the future value of membership exceeded what could be gained from a single act of fraud, honesty was self-enforcing. Courts were unnecessary; reputation did the work.

The story was attractive for reasons that went beyond the archive. It offered an elegant demonstration that institutions need not be imposed from above, that cooperation could be sustained by self-interest alone, and it supplied a template for thinking about developing economies in which formal enforcement is weak. Informal networks, it suggested, were not a primitive substitute for law but an efficient solution in their own right.

Later scholars who returned to the same letters found a messier picture. The merchants, it turned out, did use courts, drew up formal partnerships, deposited documents with notaries and threatened litigation when correspondence failed. Agents were by no means drawn exclusively from within the network, and the evidence that collective punishment of cheaters was ever systematically applied proved thin. Reputation mattered, but it operated alongside legal mechanisms rather than in place of them. The critics went further: the very fluidity that made the network attractive to the theory — merchants moving between associates as opportunity dictated — is hard to reconcile with the dense, closed membership on which multilateral punishment depends.

It would be a mistake, though, to read this revision as a simple victory of law over trust. Courts in this period were slow, costly and uncertain, and their judgments were difficult to enforce across jurisdictions. A merchant who sued a distant agent might win a verdict and recover nothing. What the litigants seem to have valued in legal procedure was frequently not coercion but documentation: a notarised contract created a public record that could be shown to third parties, so that formal institutions extended the reach of reputation rather than replacing it. Equally, reputational sanctions were credible partly because the threat of litigation stood behind them.

The broader lesson concerns how theories are tested against history. A model that explains an outcome by a single mechanism will tend, when it searches the archive, to find that mechanism; the letters that discuss reputation are vivid and quotable, while the routine traces of legal practice are easy to overlook. The danger is not that such a model is false but that its elegance comes to be treated as evidence for it. Institutions in the past, like institutions now, were seldom pure types. They were layered arrangements in which private and public enforcement leaned on each other, and their success depended less on any one device than on the way the devices were combined.

passages.title: Passage: The mirror test
passages.text:
For half a century the mirror test has served as comparative psychology's most famous gatekeeper. An animal is marked, without its knowledge, on a part of its body it can see only in a reflection; if, on facing a mirror, it inspects or tries to remove the mark, it is credited with recognising the reflection as itself. Great apes pass, as do some dolphins, an elephant or two and the Eurasian magpie. Dogs, cats and most monkeys, by and large, do not. The test's appeal lies in its apparent cleanness: it asks a yes-or-no question and seems to answer it without any need to interpret the animal's inner life.

That cleanness has always been partly an illusion. A pass requires not one capacity but several: the animal must attend to mirrors at all, care about an anomaly on its body, and possess a repertoire of movements that allows it to investigate the mark. An animal that relies chiefly on smell, as dogs do, may simply find a visual image uninteresting; an animal for which grooming is not a natural response to a blemish has no obvious reason to touch it. Failures are therefore hard to read. Passes, it was long assumed, were not.

That assumption came under strain when a small reef fish, the cleaner wrasse, which makes its living removing parasites from other fish, was reported to scrape a coloured mark against the sea floor after viewing it in a mirror — and to ignore an identical mark it could not see. By the test's own criteria, the fish had passed. The reaction among researchers was instructive. Some concluded that self-recognition must be far more widespread than supposed; others concluded that the test must measure something less than self-recognition, since it could not be that a fish possessed a self-concept comparable to a chimpanzee's. Both responses accepted the result; they differed on which of their prior commitments to give up.

The second response deserves more sympathy than it is sometimes given, though not for the reason usually offered. The trouble is not that fish are too lowly to have selves, a judgement that begs the very question at issue. It is that the test was never validated as a measure of a self-concept in the first place. It was designed with primates in mind, calibrated on primates and interpreted through a picture of the self — reflective, unified, able to take itself as an object — that was itself derived from human introspection. A behaviour that tracks that capacity in apes may be produced by quite different machinery in a species whose ecology rewards close attention to marks on bodies.

None of this means the wrasse result should be dismissed. It means that a single behavioural criterion cannot carry the theoretical weight that has been placed on it. What the episode recommends is not a lower bar or a higher one but a plurality of tests, each fitted to the perceptual world and behavioural repertoire of the species examined, whose convergence — or failure to converge — would tell us more than any one of them could. Comparative cognition has often progressed by asking whether animals can do what we do. It may progress further by asking what, given the lives they lead, it would even mean for them to do it.

passages.title: Passage: Authenticity and the rebuilt shrine
passages.text:
Every twenty years, in a ceremony that has been performed with few interruptions for some thirteen centuries, the principal buildings of the Ise shrine in Japan are dismantled and rebuilt on an adjacent plot, using fresh cypress and the same techniques. Visitors from Europe have often been puzzled by the custom. Is the shrine they see thirteen centuries old or a few years old? The question seems to admit of an answer only if one has already decided what makes a building the building it is — its material, its form or the unbroken practice that reproduces it.

The European conservation tradition, at least since the nineteenth century, has largely answered in favour of material. Its guiding horror is the restoration that replaces original fabric with conjectural copy, and its guiding virtue is the honesty with which later interventions are distinguished from what survives. A cathedral repaired with new stone is expected to show the joins. Behind this lies a conception of the monument as a document: an object whose value consists in the evidence it carries of the past, and which is falsified, like a forged charter, if its substance is silently renewed.

Ise suggests a different conception, in which what is transmitted is not an object but a competence. The carpenters who rebuild the shrine are the custodians of knowledge that exists only in their hands and must be exercised to survive; a building preserved untouched for a thousand years would preserve the form while losing the skill. On this view, the periodic destruction of the material is not a threat to authenticity but its condition. Authenticity resides in the continuity of a living practice rather than in the persistence of particular atoms.

It is tempting to turn this contrast into a parable about East and West, but the parable flatters both sides. Japanese practice has never been uniform — many temples are prized precisely for their ancient timbers — and European cities are full of buildings whose 'original' fabric is the product of repeated, unacknowledged repair. More importantly, the documentary conception has itself shifted. International conservation charters now concede that authenticity may be judged differently in different cultural contexts and that it can attach to traditions, techniques and settings as well as to materials. The concession was hard won, and its critics fear that it dissolves the concept: if anything that continues a tradition can count as authentic, the word risks ceasing to discriminate at all.

That fear is reasonable, but it misidentifies the danger. The question is not whether authenticity should be located in matter or in practice, as if one answer were correct everywhere, but what a particular community is trying to keep faith with. A medieval charter and a living craft make different claims on us, and a conservation ethic adequate to both must ask, case by case, what is being handed on and what would count as betraying it. Such an ethic is harder to codify than a rule about original fabric. It is also, perhaps, the only one that does not mistake the means of preservation for its end.

passages.title: Set: Five-team league
passages.text:
Five teams — A, B, C, D and E — played a single round-robin football tournament, in which every pair of teams met exactly once. A win earned 3 points, a draw 1 point and a loss 0 points. When the tournament ended, the following were known:

1. No two teams finished with the same number of points.
2. A finished first, B second, C third, D fourth and E fifth.
3. Every team won at least one match.

passages.title: Set: On-call roster
passages.text:
A hospital roster puts exactly two of four doctors — A, B, C and D — on call on each day of a week, from Monday to Sunday. Over the week, A was on call on five days, and each of B, C and D on three days. The following are also known:

1. No doctor was on call on three consecutive days. (Sunday and the following Monday are not considered consecutive.)
2. B was on call on Monday and on Sunday.
3. A and C were on call together on exactly two days.

passages.title: Set: A four-round number game
passages.text:
Three players — X, Y and Z — played a game of four rounds. In each round, each player secretly wrote one of the numbers 1, 2 or 3, and the numbers were then revealed together. In a round, a player scored the number he had written if no other player had written the same number in that round; otherwise he scored nothing in that round.

No player wrote the same number in two consecutive rounds. At the end of the four rounds, X had 10 points, Y had 6 points and Z had 4 points.

passages.title: Set: Judges and dishes
passages.text:
Four judges — W, X, Y and Z — each rated three dishes, P, Q and R, in a cooking contest. Every rating was an integer from 1 to 5, and no judge gave the same rating to two different dishes. The following are also known:

1. The total ratings received by P, Q and R were 15, 12 and 9 respectively.
2. The totals of the four judges (the sum of the three ratings each gave) were all different. W's total, 12, was the highest and Z's total, 6, was the lowest; X's total was higher than Y's.
3. Each dish received a rating of 5 from at least one judge.

passages.title: Set: Online courses
passages.text: Each of the 120 employees of a firm completed at least one of three online courses — Python, SQL and Excel. 70 employees completed Python, 60 completed SQL and 50 completed Excel. The number of employees who completed exactly two of the three courses was twice the number who completed all three. Each of the three groups of employees who completed exactly two courses (Python and SQL only; Python and Excel only; SQL and Excel only) had at least 5 members.

questions.question: A trader marks an article 40% above its cost price and then allows two successive discounts of 10% and x%. If he still makes a profit of 13.4%, what is x?

relevance.note: Mark-up 40%, discounts 10% & x%, profit 13.4% -> x=10; CAT-standard numbers and distractors

questions.question: For how many integer values of k does the equation x² + kx + 16 = 0 have no real roots?
questions.explanation: No real roots ⇔ k² − 64 < 0 ⇔ −8 < k < 8, i.e. k = −7, …, 7: 15 integers.

relevance.note: Discriminant k^2<64 -> 15 integers, off-by-one distractors 14/16/17; CAT-typical

questions.question: How many integers x satisfy |x − 2| + |x + 3| ≤ 9?
questions.explanation: For −3 ≤ x ≤ 2 the sum is 5 (valid). For x > 2: 2x + 1 ≤ 9 → x ≤ 4. For x < −3: −2x − 1 ≤ 9 → x ≥ −5. So −5 ≤ x ≤ 4: 10 integers.

relevance.note: |x-2|+|x+3|<=9 gives -5..4 = 10 integers; exact CAT modulus-count format

questions.question: Let f(x) = 2x + 3 and g(x) = x² − 1. What is the sum of all real values of x for which f(g(x)) = g(f(x))?
questions.explanation: f(g(x)) = 2x² + 1; g(f(x)) = (2x + 3)² − 1 = 4x² + 12x + 8. Equating: 2x² + 12x + 7 = 0, discriminant 144 − 56 = 88 > 0, so both roots are real; sum = −12/2 = −6.

relevance.note: f(g)=g(f) -> 2x^2+12x+7=0, sum -6; CAT functions style with sign trap

questions.question: What is the remainder when 7¹⁰⁰ is divided by 13?

relevance.note: 7^100 mod 13 via Fermat = 9; CAT remainder archetype

questions.question: How many four-digit numbers with all digits distinct can be formed using the digits 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 that are divisible by 5?
questions.explanation: Ending in 0: remaining three places from 5 digits in order = 5 × 4 × 3 = 60. Ending in 5: first digit from {1, 2, 3, 4} (cannot be 0) = 4 ways, then 4 × 3 = 12 for the middle → 48. Total 108.

relevance.note: 4-digit distinct from 0-5 divisible by 5 = 108 with 0-case trap; CAT-typical

questions.question:
Five teams—A, B, C, D and E—played a single round-robin tournament, each pair meeting once. A win earned 2 points, a draw 1 point and a loss 0 points. The final points were: A 7, B 5, C 4, D 3, E 1.

What is the minimum possible number of drawn matches in the tournament?
questions.explanation: Every draw gives 1 point to each of two teams, so a team with an odd total has an odd number of draws. A, B, D and E have odd totals, so each drew at least once; that is at least 4 team-draws, i.e. at least 2 drawn matches. Two is achievable, e.g. draws A–E and B–D with A beating B, C, D; B beating C, E; C beating D, E; D beating E.

relevance.note: Min draws for 7/5/4/3/1 = 2 verified by full enumeration of 3^10 outcomes; faithful CAT tournament reasoning

questions.question:
Eight players seeded 1 (strongest) to 8 play a knockout tournament. Quarter-finals: 1 v 8, 4 v 5, 2 v 7, 3 v 6. Semi-finals: winner(1 v 8) v winner(4 v 5), and winner(2 v 7) v winner(3 v 6). A match is an 'upset' if the higher-numbered seed wins.
• There were exactly three upsets in the tournament.
• Seed 3 won the tournament.
• Seed 1 reached the final.
• Seed 2 lost its first match.

Which seed did the runner-up defeat in the semi-final?
questions.explanation: Seed 1 is the runner-up. Upsets so far: 7 beat 2 (QF) and 3 beat 1 (final). 3 beating 7 in the semi is not an upset, nor is 1 beating 8 or 1 beating 4/5 in the semi. The third upset must be 5 beating 4 in the quarter-final, so seed 1 beat seed 5 in the semi-final.

relevance.note: Bracket with 3 upsets, unique reconstruction (runner-up 1 beat 5) verified; mirrors CAT upset sets

questions.question: A shopkeeper marks his goods 50% above cost price, allows a discount of d% on the marked price, and also uses a false weight of 900 g in place of 1 kg. If his overall profit is 20%, what is d?
questions.explanation: Let 1 kg cost ₹100. He delivers 900 g (cost ₹90) and charges 150(1 − d/100). Profit 20% on ₹90 means selling price = ₹108, so 1 − d/100 = 108/150 = 0.72, d = 28.

relevance.note: Mark-up 50%, false weight 900 g, profit 20% -> d=28; CAT-style false-weight combo

questions.question: How many ordered pairs of positive integers (x, y) satisfy 3x + 5y = 101?
questions.explanation: 3x = 101 − 5y must be a positive multiple of 3, so 5y ≡ 101 ≡ 2 (mod 3), i.e. y ≡ 1 (mod 3). y = 1, 4, 7, 10, 13, 16, 19 (y = 19 gives x = 2; y = 22 makes x negative): 7 pairs.

relevance.note: 3x+5y=101 has 7 positive solutions; signature CAT Diophantine count

questions.question: For how many integer values of x is |x − 5| + |x + 1| = 6?
options: Infinitely many
questions.explanation: The sum of distances from x to 5 and to −1 equals the distance between them, 6, exactly when −1 ≤ x ≤ 5. The integers −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 give 7 values.

relevance.note: |x-5|+|x+1|=6 holds on whole [-1,5] = 7 integers, 'only 2' trap; exact CAT whole-interval trap

questions.question: Let f(x) = min(2x + 3, 15 − x) for all real x. What is the maximum value of f(x)?
questions.explanation: 2x + 3 increases and 15 − x decreases, so the minimum of the two is largest where they are equal: 2x + 3 = 15 − x gives x = 4 and f = 11.

relevance.note: max of min(2x+3,15-x) at x=4 gives 11; CAT functions archetype

questions.question: What is the remainder when 17²³ + 23²³ is divided by 40?
questions.explanation: For odd n, aⁿ + bⁿ is divisible by a + b. Here a + b = 40, so the remainder is 0.

relevance.note: 17^23+23^23 divisible by 40 (odd power a+b); CAT number-system archetype

questions.question: Which of the following best captures the central argument of the passage?
options: Since no individual can verify most of what she believes, the ideal of intellectual autonomy should give way to a default entitlement to trust what others assert.
Testimony is a basic source of knowledge, like perception, but it needs to be supplemented by institutions that expose insincere or incompetent speakers.
Neither the demand for first-hand backing nor a default entitlement to trust adequately explains testimonial knowledge, whose justification rests largely on social structures that screen claims.
Reductionism fails because children acquire their concepts through trust, which shows that testimony is a more dependable source of knowledge than first-hand observation.
questions.explanation: The author rejects reductionism (the ledger never balances) and also finds anti-reductionism too permissive (it licenses gullibility), then relocates the warrant in institutions that filter claims. Option 1 is the Reid-style view the author criticises. Option 2 keeps Reid's "basic faculty" claim, which the author does not endorse, and narrows institutions to catching liars. Option 4 distorts the child example: it shows reductionism cannot work, not that testimony is more dependable than observation.

relevance.note: Epistemology-of-testimony RC central idea; distractors over-generalise (0) or adopt Reid's view (1) as in CAT 2024 philosophy passages

questions.question: The author would most likely agree with which of the following statements?
options: A belief acquired through testimony is justified only if the hearer can name the institution that vetted it.
A person may become less justified in holding a belief she has not changed, if the institutions that vetted the belief decline.
Once institutional filters are in place, an individual's own scrutiny of what she is told becomes epistemically irrelevant.
The anti-reductionist view is mistaken chiefly because people rarely encounter defeaters in ordinary life.
questions.explanation: The last paragraph says the erosion of institutions "quietly drains the justification from beliefs I continue to hold, without my noticing" — exactly option 2. Option 1 demands something the author never requires (the hearer need not identify the filter). Option 3 is an extreme the author does not state. Option 4 invents a reason; the author's objection is that the view licenses gullibility.

relevance.note: 'Would agree' keyed on the eroding-institutions corollary; extreme distractors (0,2) mirror CAT inference traps

questions.question: The author mentions an adult who sets out to verify the reliability of encyclopaedias in order to
options: contrast the adult's capacity for independent checking with a child's dependence on others.
suggest that reference works are less reliable than their readers commonly assume.
show that inductive reasoning cannot establish anything about the reliability of sources.
show that any attempt to back testimony with one's own investigation would itself have to rely on testimony.
questions.explanation: The example extends the child case ("Even an adult…"): checking encyclopaedias would require testimony about which exist and how their errors were found, so the reductionist's ledger cannot be balanced. Option 1 reverses its role (the adult is no better off). Option 2 is about the content of the example, not its role. Option 3 overstates: the author says the inductive base is too narrow, not that induction is useless.

relevance.note: Function-of-example question on the encyclopaedia case; a CAT staple, slightly easier than 2024 function items

questions.question: The passage is primarily concerned with
options: arguing that medieval merchants relied on courts rather than on reputation to discipline their overseas agents.
explaining why informal networks can be an efficient substitute for law in economies where the state is weak.
criticising historians for preferring vivid, quotable letters to routine legal documents.
revising an influential account of medieval trade by showing that informal and formal enforcement supported each other.
questions.explanation: The passage presents the reputation-only story, reports the critics' evidence of legal practice, then refuses to see this as "a simple victory of law over trust", concluding that private and public enforcement "leaned on each other". Option 1 is the reading the author explicitly warns against. Option 2 is the original account being revised. Option 3 is a detail from the last paragraph, too narrow to be the primary concern.

relevance.note: Primary-concern question on the revisionist medieval-trade passage; options 0/1 are the classic one-sided traps

questions.question: Which of the following is most consistent with the account given in the fourth paragraph?
options: Merchants who went to court cared less about their reputation than merchants who avoided litigation.
A merchant might have a contract notarised even if he did not expect a court to enforce it against a distant agent.
The threat of collective punishment was ineffective because merchants frequently changed their associates.
Courts were of little value to medieval merchants, since their verdicts could rarely be enforced across jurisdictions.
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph says litigants valued legal procedure "frequently not [for] coercion but documentation": a notarised contract created a record that could be shown to third parties. So a merchant could want notarisation without expecting enforcement. Option 1 contradicts the complementarity described. Option 3 overstates the critics' point (fluidity is "hard to reconcile" with multilateral punishment; the passage does not say punishment was ineffective). Option 4 ignores the documentary value the paragraph stresses.

relevance.note: Paragraph-specific inference (notarised contract as documentation) - close to CAT 2023 econ-history RC

questions.question: Which of the following findings, if it came from the merchants' letters, would most seriously weaken the account described in the first paragraph?
options: Courts in Palermo seldom ruled in favour of merchants from abroad.
Most agents were recruited from among the members of the merchants' own network.
Agents known to have cheated one member of the network continued to receive commissions from other members.
Letters discussing the honesty of particular agents far outnumber letters discussing lawsuits.
questions.explanation: The original account rests on multilateral punishment: a cheat of any member is shunned by all, which makes honesty self-enforcing. Evidence that known cheats kept getting business from other members attacks exactly that mechanism. Options 1, 2 and 4 are all consistent with, or supportive of, the original story (courts unreliable, closed membership, reputation as the main concern).

relevance.note: Weaken the reputation-coalition model: cheaters not shunned attacks the mechanism; good CAT-level weaken

questions.question: The final paragraph of the passage serves mainly to
options: draw a methodological caution about how an elegant single-cause explanation can shape the evidence its proponents notice.
concede that the original account was correct in its essentials despite the evidence its critics produced.
argue that surviving archives are too fragmentary to settle debates about how past institutions worked.
suggest that modern institutions differ from medieval ones in combining private and public enforcement.
questions.explanation: The paragraph turns to "how theories are tested against history": a single-mechanism model tends to find its mechanism, and its elegance comes to be treated as evidence. Option 2 contradicts the revision the passage accepts. Option 3 goes beyond the text (the problem is selective attention, not fragmentary archives). Option 4 reverses the comparison: institutions "in the past, like institutions now" were layered.

relevance.note: Function of final paragraph (methodological caution); distractors plausible, CAT-faithful

questions.question: The author would most likely agree that a dog's failure in the mirror test

proves that the test is invalid for every species other than the primates on which it was calibrated.
would turn into a pass if the test used an odour mark instead of a visual one.
is compatible with the dog's possessing some form of self-recognition that the test is not suited to detect.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says failures are "hard to read" because a pass needs several capacities; a dog, relying on smell, "may simply find a visual image uninteresting". So failure does not rule out self-recognition. Option 1 is the inference the author rejects. Option 2 is far stronger than the author's claim. Option 3 asserts a definite outcome the author never predicts; she recommends species-fitted tests without saying what they would show.

relevance.note: Inference on dog's failure; option 2 over-commits to odour test - typical CAT trap

questions.question: The author describes the two reactions of researchers to the cleaner wrasse result primarily in order to
options: show that an unexpected pass forced researchers to give up either a belief about which animals have selves or a belief about what the test measures.
suggest that researchers who doubted the result were motivated by prejudice against fish.
illustrate the disagreement over whether the wrasse had actually scraped off the mark.
demonstrate that self-recognition is more widespread in the animal kingdom than primatologists believed.
questions.explanation: The author notes that "both responses accepted the result; they differed on which of their prior commitments to give up" — the point of describing them. Option 2 confuses the later remark about question-begging with the purpose of the description, and no one doubted the result. Option 3 is wrong for the same reason. Option 4 states only one of the two reactions, which the author does not endorse.

relevance.note: Purpose of citing two researcher reactions; clean function item

questions.question: The passage suggests each of the following as a possible reason why an animal might fail the mirror test EXCEPT that the animal
options: pays little attention to visual images in mirrors.
does not respond to a blemish on its body by grooming.
belongs to a species whose way of life rewards close attention to marks on bodies.
lacks movements suited to investigating a mark it has noticed.
questions.explanation: Options 1, 2 and 4 restate the three capacities listed in the second paragraph whose absence could cause a failure. Option 3 comes from the fourth paragraph, where an ecology that rewards attention to marks is offered as a reason a species (the wrasse) might pass without a primate-like self-concept — the opposite role.

relevance.note: EXCEPT detail check (ecology rewarding mark attention is a pass-reason); fits CAT detail items, a bit easy

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the view that the mirror test measures something less than self-recognition is best described as
options: unreserved endorsement, treating it as the only reasonable response to the wrasse result.
qualified support, accepting its conclusion while rejecting the justification usually given for it.
measured scepticism, regarding it as a defensive reaction that begs the question at issue.
cautious rejection, granting its premise while denying that it follows from the wrasse result.
questions.explanation: The author says the second response "deserves more sympathy than it is sometimes given, though not for the reason usually offered": the usual reason (fish are too lowly) begs the question, but the conclusion is supported by the fact that the test was never validated as a measure of a self-concept. Option 3 applies the "begs the question" charge to the view itself rather than to its usual justification. Options 1 and 4 misstate the degree of support.

relevance.note: Attitude question with paired adjectives ('qualified support' vs 'measured scepticism'), exactly CAT tone format

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the main point of the passage?
options: The rebuilding of Ise shows that authenticity lies in living traditions rather than in surviving material, a lesson European conservation has belatedly accepted.
European and Japanese approaches to conservation are fundamentally opposed because they reflect different cultural conceptions of the past.
Whether a renewed structure is authentic depends on what its tradition seeks to hand on, so neither material nor practice can serve as the criterion everywhere.
By extending authenticity to traditions and techniques, international charters have made the concept too broad to distinguish genuine monuments from spurious ones.

Option 1 makes practice the universal answer, which the author denies. Option 2 is the East-West "parable" the author says flatters both sides. Option 4 is the critics' fear, which the author calls reasonable but misdirected.

questions.question: In the context of the passage, an ethic that "mistake[s] the means of preservation for its end" would
options: confuse the techniques used by conservators with the aesthetic qualities of the monuments they repair.
treat the retention of original material as valuable in itself rather than as one way of keeping faith with what a community wishes to pass on.
insist that a building be preserved for ever when its purpose is to be periodically replaced.
value the documentation of interventions more highly than the interventions themselves.
questions.explanation: The sentence contrasts a codifiable "rule about original fabric" with an ethic that asks what is being handed on. Keeping original material is a means; keeping faith with what is transmitted is the end. Option 3 reads the phrase only in terms of Ise and makes it a claim about building purpose. Options 1 and 4 import distinctions (aesthetics, documentation versus intervention) that the passage does not draw.

relevance.note: Meaning of closing phrase in context; good abstraction level

questions.question: The author observes that many Japanese temples are prized for their ancient timbers in order to
options: show that the Ise custom is an exception that most Japanese builders have rejected.
suggest that Japanese conservation is gradually moving towards the European documentary model.
establish that the material conception of authenticity is in fact universal.
undermine the idea that the contrast between material and practice corresponds neatly to a contrast between European and Japanese culture.
questions.explanation: The remark is offered as evidence that "Japanese practice has never been uniform", alongside unacknowledged repair in Europe — both against turning the contrast into "a parable about East and West". Option 1 overstates (non-uniform, not rejected). Option 2 invents a trend. Option 3 is contradicted by the rest of the passage.

relevance.note: Role of Japanese-timbers detail in undercutting East/West parable; good CAT function item

questions.question: It can be inferred that a conservator committed to the "documentary" conception described in the passage would most likely object to
options: stabilising a crumbling wall with modern mortar that is visibly different from the original.
displaying a surviving fragment of a fresco beside a clearly labelled modern reconstruction.
replacing a decayed carved panel with an exact replica without recording or marking that it is new.
leaving a damaged medieval charter unrestored so that its condition can be studied.
questions.explanation: On the documentary view a monument is "falsified, like a forged charter, if its substance is silently renewed", and later interventions must be distinguished from what survives. An unmarked, unrecorded replica is exactly such silent renewal. Options 1 and 2 show the joins, which the view requires; option 4 preserves the evidence untouched.

relevance.note: Application inference for documentary conservator; a little easy as option 2 is clearly flagged

questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Historians are often warned off counterfactuals as idle speculation: what would have happened had the monsoon not failed in a given year, or had a particular general survived a battle, is unknowable, and the professional historian deals in what happened. Yet every causal claim a historian makes is implicitly counterfactual. To say that a famine was caused by export policy rather than by drought is to say that, had the policy been different, the famine would have been less severe — a claim about a world that never existed. The choice, then, is not between using counterfactuals and avoiding them, but between using them openly, where their assumptions can be examined, and using them silently, where they cannot.
options: Historians should abandon causal claims about events such as famines, since such claims depend on alternative worlds that cannot be known.
Counterfactual reasoning is legitimate in history only when it concerns policy choices rather than natural events such as drought.
Although counterfactuals are unknowable, historians rely on them because explicit speculation makes historical explanation more persuasive.
Because historical explanation necessarily rests on claims about what would otherwise have happened, historians should state such claims explicitly so that they can be scrutinised.
questions.explanation: The paragraph argues that causal claims are implicitly counterfactual, so the real choice is between explicit (examinable) and silent use. Option 1 draws the opposite conclusion. Option 2 adds a policy/nature distinction that the famine example does not make. Option 3 supplies a motive (persuasiveness) the passage never gives.

relevance.note: Para summary with too-extreme/too-narrow distractors, same format as CAT 2023-25 summary items

questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Linguists who document an endangered language — recording its last fluent speakers, compiling a grammar and a dictionary — are sometimes said to be "saving" it. The metaphor misleads. A language survives not in an archive but in the decisions of parents about what to speak to their children, and those decisions respond to schools, markets and prestige far more than to the existence of a reference grammar. Documentation can preserve a record of a language and can supply materials to a community that decides to revive it; what it cannot do is supply the decision.
options: Recording an endangered language preserves a resource that can aid a revival, but whether the language lives depends on choices to pass it on, which are shaped by social forces.
Documenting endangered languages is of little value, since a language survives only when parents choose to speak it to their children.
Endangered languages can be saved if linguists provide their communities with grammars and dictionaries before the last speakers die.
Parents abandon endangered languages mainly because schools and markets reward dominant languages, and linguists should campaign against these pressures.
questions.explanation: The paragraph grants documentation a real but limited role (a record and materials for revival) while locating survival in transmission decisions driven by schools, markets and prestige. Option 2 overstates by denying documentation any value. Option 3 is the "saving" metaphor the author rejects. Option 4 adds a prescription for linguists that the passage does not make.

relevance.note: Para summary on language documentation; option 1 'little value' over-states - real CAT trap

questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Each prescription of an antibiotic is, for the patient who receives it, a reasonable bet: the drug will probably help and the harm it does to that patient is small. But each use also exerts selective pressure that favours resistant bacteria, and that cost is borne not by the patient or the prescriber but by everyone who will later need the drug to work. Resistance is thus less a medical failure than a problem of shared resources: an effective antibiotic is a common good depleted by individually rational use, and no amount of exhortation to individual doctors will substitute for arrangements that bring the collective cost into individual decisions.
options: Doctors over-prescribe antibiotics because they underestimate the harm the drugs do to the individual patients who take them.
Since every prescription harms future patients, antibiotics should be reserved for cases in which a patient's life is at risk.

As the benefit of each antibiotic prescription goes to the patient while the cost of resistance is spread over everyone, curbing resistance needs institutional arrangements, not merely appeals to prescribers.
Antibiotic resistance is fundamentally a medical failure that can be overcome only by developing new drugs faster than bacteria adapt.
questions.explanation: The paragraph frames resistance as a commons problem — individually rational use depletes a shared good — and concludes that exhortation cannot replace arrangements that internalise the collective cost. Option 1 contradicts "individually rational" use. Option 2 offers a rule the passage never proposes. Option 4 contradicts "less a medical failure".

relevance.note: Antibiotic commons summary; correct but a little guessable vs CAT 2024 summaries

questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Defenders of "nudges" — default options, reminder letters, rearranged cafeteria counters — argue that since every choice must be presented in some way, there is no neutral design to retreat to; the planner may as well arrange options to help people do what they themselves would endorse on reflection. Critics reply that the argument proves too little. That some framing is unavoidable does not settle who should choose it, and the standard of what people "would endorse on reflection" is supplied, in practice, by the very officials whose judgement is in question. The inevitability of influence does not by itself legitimise any particular use of it.
options: Because every choice is framed in some way, nudges are unavoidable and should be designed to reflect people's considered preferences.
Even if choices cannot be presented neutrally, it does not follow that officials are entitled to frame them according to their own estimate of what people would endorse.
Nudges are illegitimate because they manipulate people into choices they would reject on reflection.
Critics of nudges deny that every choice must be framed and argue instead for neutral ways of presenting options.
questions.explanation: The paragraph reports the defenders' argument and then the critics' reply, which is its point: unavoidable framing does not settle who frames, and the "reflective endorsement" standard is supplied by the officials themselves. Option 1 is only the defenders' view. Option 3 is more extreme than the critics' claim. Option 4 misstates the critics, who accept that framing is unavoidable.

relevance.note: Nudge summary where critic's view must be captured - hard, very CAT-like

questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

A map that recorded every feature of the terrain would be as large as the terrain and as useless. Cartographers therefore do not merely record; they decide what to leave out, and those decisions encode a purpose — navigation, taxation, military planning — that the finished map rarely announces. A map's authority comes from its appearance of neutral description, which is why its omissions are so easily mistaken for absences in the world itself. Reading a map well means asking not only whether it is accurate but for whom, and for what, it was drawn.
options: Maps are unreliable because cartographers deliberately leave out features that would conflict with the interests of those who commission them.
Maps drawn for taxation or military planning tend to be less accurate than maps drawn for navigation.
The most useful maps are those that omit the most detail, since a complete map would be unusable.
Since every map is shaped by purposeful choices about what to omit, its apparent neutrality should not be taken at face value and its purpose should inform how it is read.
questions.explanation: The paragraph moves from the necessity of omission, to the purpose encoded in omissions, to the hidden nature of that purpose behind apparent neutrality, and ends with how to read maps. Option 1 turns purpose into deliberate concealment and calls maps unreliable, beyond the text. Option 2 compares accuracy across purposes, which the passage never does. Option 3 distorts the opening point into a ranking of maps.

relevance.note: Maps-and-purpose summary; distractors extreme/narrow; slightly easy

questions.question:
The 4 sentences given below, labelled 1 to 4, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order and key in the sequence of numbers as your answer (for example, 2143).

1. It is therefore possible for such a table to reward exclusion and penalise inclusion while appearing merely to report results.
2. League tables of schools typically rank institutions by the average examination score of their pupils.
3. Such a ranking, however, says nothing about how a school arrived at its average.
4. A school whose average rises may simply have admitted fewer weak pupils, while one whose average falls may have taken in more of them and supported them well.

questions.question:
The 4 sentences given below, labelled 1 to 4, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order and key in the sequence of numbers as your answer (for example, 2143).

1. The placebo effect was long explained as a product of deception: the patient improves because she believes she is receiving an active drug.
2. If so, the ethical objection that has kept placebos out of routine practice — that they require doctors to lie — may be weaker than supposed.
3. On this account, it is the expectation of relief, not the substance itself, that does the work.

questions.question:
The 4 sentences given below, labelled 1 to 4, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper order and key in the sequence of numbers as your answer (for example, 2143).

1. Firms adopted them on a vast scale, persuaded that chance encounters between colleagues would spark collaboration.
2. Deprived of privacy, workers seem to have built invisible walls of their own, retreating into headphones and screens.
3. Open-plan offices were sold on the promise that removing walls would bring colleagues together.

questions.question:
Five jumbled sentences, labelled 1 to 5, are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the sentence that does not fit and key in its number as your answer.

1. The first coins, struck in Lydia in the seventh century BCE, were lumps of electrum stamped with a lion's head.
2. The Lydians were also credited by Herodotus with opening the first permanent retail shops.
3. Because natural electrum varied in its gold content, the value of a lump could not be read from its weight alone.
4. The stamp therefore guaranteed not purity so much as identity: it declared who stood behind the metal.

Five jumbled sentences, labelled 1 to 5, are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the sentence that does not fit and key in its number as your answer.

2. Their data are noisy, since observers differ in skill and effort, but the sheer number of observations allows much of that variation to be corrected statistically.

4. Some economists argue that targeting the growth of nominal GDP instead would cushion economies better against supply shocks.

questions.question: How many points did E score?
questions.explanation: E won at least one match, so E ≥ 3. If E ≥ 4, the five different totals would be at least 4 + 5 + 6 + 7 + 8 = 30. But each match gives out 3 points (win) or 2 points (draw), so the grand total is 30 − (number of draws) ≤ 30. A total of 30 would mean no draws, making every team's total a multiple of 3; five different multiples of 3, each at least 4, add up to far more than 30. Hence E = 3.

relevance.note: Round-robin W/D/L league, verified 26 cases all give E=3; CAT 2023-24 tournament style

questions.question: What is the maximum possible number of matches that ended in a draw?
questions.explanation: Totals are at least 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 (sum 25), and the grand total is 30 − draws, so draws ≤ 5. Five draws would force totals of exactly A 7, B 6, C 5, D 4, E 3. Then E (3 points with a win) has no draws, D (4) has 1, C (5 = 1W + 2D) has 2, B (6) has 0 or 3, A (7) has 1 or 4. Team-draws must equal 2 × 5 = 10, which needs B = 3 and A = 4 draws; but A drawing all four matches includes a draw with E, who has none — impossible. Four draws is achievable: A–B, A–C, B–C and B–D drawn; A beat D and E, B beat E, C beat D, D beat E and E beat C, giving A 8, B 6, C 5, D 4, E 3. Hence 4.

relevance.note: Max draws under distinct points; brute force gives 4; good CAT difficulty

questions.question: If A scored 10 points, which of the following must be true?
options: C drew with D.
B beat E.
D beat E.
A drew with B.
questions.explanation: A = 10 means 3 wins and 1 draw; E = 3 has no draw and D = 4 has exactly one. With k draws, 30 − k = 10 + B + C + 4 + 3, so B + C = 13 − k, and B + C ≥ 6 + 5 gives k ≤ 2. If k = 1, that draw is A–D, so B and C have no draws and their totals are different multiples of 3 adding to 12 — impossible. So k = 2 and B + C = 11, i.e. B = 6, C = 5 (= 1 win + 2 draws). The four team-draws are A's one, D's one and C's two, so C drew with A and with D. Results such as B–E and D–E can go either way, and A beat B.

relevance.note: Conditional must-be-true (A=10 -> C drew D) verified over 3 cases

questions.question: If exactly three matches ended in a draw, which pair of teams must have drawn their match?
options: A and D
B and C
C and D
A and C
questions.explanation: Grand total = 27, with E = 3 and D = 4, so A + B + C = 20 with A > B > C ≥ 5. (9, 6, 5) fails: A = 9 has no draws, so B would need 3 draws (with C, D, E), but E has none. So A 8 (2W 2D), B 7 (2W 1D), C 5 (1W 2D), D 4 (1 draw), E none. A's two draws are with two of B, C, D. If A drew with B and D, both would have used up their only draw and C could find no partners for its two draws. Hence A drew with C. (A–D, B–C and C–D can each go either way.)

relevance.note: Exactly 3 draws forces A-C draw (5 cases); CAT-faithful

questions.question: Which of the following could NOT have happened in the tournament?
options: A lost to C.
B lost to E.
D drew with E.
B drew with C.
questions.explanation: E scored exactly 3 points with at least one win, so E won once and lost three times — E drew no match, so D–E was not a draw. Each of the other results occurs in some valid table, e.g. A 9 (losing to C), B 7, C 6, D 4, E 3; or A 10, B 6 (losing to E), C 5, D 4, E 3; or A 9, B 7 (drawing with C), C 5, D 4, E 3.

relevance.note: Could-NOT-happen: D-E draw impossible; verified

questions.question: On which of the following days was A definitely on call?
options: Tuesday
Wednesday
Thursday
Friday
questions.explanation: If A were off on Monday, A's five days would lie within the six consecutive days Tuesday–Sunday, and any five of six consecutive days include three in a row. So A is on call on Monday, and by the same argument on Sunday — on both days with B. A's other three days lie in Tuesday–Saturday, cannot include both Tuesday and Wednesday (Mon–Tue–Wed) or both Friday and Saturday (Fri–Sat–Sun), so they are one of Tue/Wed, one of Fri/Sat, and Thursday.

relevance.note: Roster scheduling, 8 schedules enumerated; A always on Mon/Thu/Sun - only Thu among options

questions.question: On how many days of the week were C and D on call together?
questions.explanation: Let AB, AC, … be the number of days each pair is on call. A: AB + AC + AD = 5 with AC = 2, so AB + AD = 3. A must be on call on Monday and Sunday (five days out of six consecutive days would include three in a row), and B is on call on both, so AB ≥ 2. If AB = 3, B's days are all with A, AD = 0 and only one day lacks A, but 7 − 5 = 2 days lack A. So AB = 2, AD = 1. The two non-A days are pairs from B, C, D; B has one day left, C has one (3 − AC), D has two (3 − AD). The only split is BD on one day and CD on the other. So CD = 1.

relevance.note: C&D together exactly 1 day in all 8 schedules; strong CAT DILR item

questions.question: If C was never on call on two consecutive days, which of the following must be true?
options: D was on call on both Wednesday and Friday.
A was on call on Friday.
B and D were on call together on Wednesday.
C and D were on call together on Saturday.
questions.explanation: Only two complete rosters satisfy all the conditions with C on non-consecutive days: Mon AB, Tue AC, Wed BD, Thu AC, Fri AD, Sat CD, Sun AB; and Mon AB, Tue CD, Wed AD, Thu AC, Fri BD, Sat AC, Sun AB. D is on call on Wednesday and Friday in both. Each of the other statements holds in only one of them.

relevance.note: Conditional reduces to 2 schedules; only option 0 holds in both; claimed archetype D04 is a loose fit

questions.question: If B was on call on Saturday, which two doctors were on call on Wednesday?
options: A and C
C and D
A and D
B and D
questions.explanation: A is on call Monday and Sunday with B, and B's third day is its only day without A, shared with D (the two days without A are one BD and one CD). So Saturday is BD and A is off on Saturday; A's middle days are therefore Thursday, Friday and one of Tuesday/Wednesday, and the other of Tuesday/Wednesday is the CD day. A on Wednesday would give A Wednesday–Thursday–Friday, three in a row, so A is on Tuesday and Wednesday is C and D. Full roster: AB, AC, CD, AD, AC, BD, AB.

relevance.note: B on Sat forces Wed = C,D; verified unique

questions.question: If A and D were on call together on Tuesday, which two doctors were on call on Saturday?
options: A and C
B and D

A and D

questions.question: In how many of the four rounds did all three players score?
questions.explanation: X cannot repeat a number in consecutive rounds, so X's best possible total is 3 + 2 + 3 + 2 = 10: X scored in every round, writing 3 and 2 alternately. In any round the points given out are 6 (all different), the lone number (1, 2 or 3) if exactly two players match, or 0. The 20 points over four rounds can only be 6 + 6 + 6 + 2. So three rounds had all three players scoring, and in the fourth only X scored (2 points).

questions.question: In the round in which only one player scored, what number did Y write?
options: Cannot be determined
questions.explanation: In that round X scored 2, so X wrote 2 and Y and Z wrote the same number, 1 or 3. X alternates 2 and 3, so the zero round's neighbouring rounds are rounds in which X wrote 3; these are all-different rounds, so in each of them Y and Z wrote 1 and 2 in some order. If Y and Z had both written 1 in the zero round, then in the neighbouring round where X wrote 3, neither could write 1 — impossible, since one of them must. So Y (and Z) wrote 3.

questions.question: If X wrote 2 in the first round, what number did Z write in the second round?

questions.explanation: X wrote 2, 3, 2, 3. The zero round (Y = Z = 3) is round 1 or 3. Y must total 6: Y gets 1 or 2 in each X = 3 round and 1 or 3 in the scoring X = 2 round, so Y scored 3 there plus 1 and 2. If round 1 were the zero round, round 3 would have Y 3, Z 1, and Z could not write 1 in rounds 2 or 4 (both adjacent to round 3), forcing Y to write 1 in both — Y = 5. So round 3 is the zero round, round 1 has Y 3, Z 1, and in round 2 Z cannot repeat 1, so Z wrote 2 (Y wrote 1).

questions.question: How many times in all did Z write the number 1?

questions.question: Which of the following must be true?
options: Y scored in every round.
Z scored in exactly two rounds.
In some round, two players wrote 1.
X never wrote 1.

Y and Z both scored nothing in one round (so neither scored in every round), and each scored in the other three rounds (so Z scored in three rounds, not two). In the zero round the shared number was 3, and in other rounds all numbers were different, so no two players ever both wrote 1.

questions.question: What was X's total?

questions.question: How many employees completed all three courses?

questions.question: What is the maximum possible number of employees who completed only Python?

Each pair group is at least 5, so the two Python pairs are at least 5 each and only Python ≤ 70 − 15 − 10 = 45. questions.question: If the number of employees who completed only SQL equals the number who completed only Excel, what is the maximum possible number who completed SQL and Excel but not Python?

questions.question: A vessel contains 60 litres of pure milk. First, x litres are drawn off and replaced with water. Then 2x litres of the resulting mixture are drawn off and replaced with water. The vessel now contains 43.2 litres of milk. What is the value of x?

questions.question: How many divisors of 10! leave a remainder of 2 when divided by 4?
questions.explanation: A number of the form 4k + 2 is 2 × (an odd number). 10! = 2⁸ × 3⁴ × 5² × 7, so such divisors are 2 × (odd divisor of 10!). Odd divisors of 10! = (4 + 1)(2 + 1)(1 + 1) = 30.

questions.question: A right-angled triangle has an inradius of 3 cm and a circumradius of 7.5 cm. What is its area, in cm²?
questions.explanation: Hypotenuse c = 2R = 15. For a right triangle r = (a + b − c)/2, so a + b = 21. a² + b² = 225, hence 2ab = 21² − 225 = 216 and area = ab/2 = 54 (the sides are 9, 12, 15).

questions.question: Two chords AB and CD of a circle intersect at right angles at a point P inside the circle. If AP = 4 cm, PB = 6 cm and CP = 3 cm, what is the radius of the circle?

questions.question: What is the area of the region in the xy-plane defined by |x| + |y − 2| ≤ 3 and y ≥ 0?

questions.question: The roots of the equation x² − (k + 1)x + 2k = 0 differ by 3. What is the product of all possible values of k?

questions.question: What is the sum of all real values of x that satisfy log₍ₓ₋₁₎(x² − 5x + 7) = 1?
